title: Choosing a sort order on the dashboard does nothing until the trader also presses "Update sort"; Design release 1 shows the select with no button beside it

finding.frontend: A secondary button labelled "Update sort" sits immediately to the right of the sort select and submits the form that carries it (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:63-82). Changing the select alone re-orders nothing; the trader has to change it and then press the button. The same pattern applies to the filter panel, whose "Search" button is the only way to apply the keyword.
finding.prototype: Design release 1's toolbar holds the results count and the sort select and nothing else (app/views/dashboard.html:231-251). There is no button beside the select and none anywhere in the filter panel, so on the face of the design a choice takes effect on its own.
finding.difference: This finding may be wrong, and the reason it is banded disputed is that Design release 1 gives no evidence its select works at all. The prototype's dashboard route reads a sort query parameter but never applies it: getDashboardViewModel (app/routes.js:7138-7255) passes the value to the select so the right option shows as chosen and into the pagination links, and orders the notification list nowhere. Nothing on the page submits the form the select sits in either — there is no button, and the prototype ships no dashboard script that submits on change, none of the twenty-one files in app/assets/javascripts mentioning the sort control. So Design release 1's sort control changes nothing whichever way it is driven, and the absent button could equally be a design decision to apply on change or an unimplemented corner of a prototype. Settle it before doing anything: if it is a design decision, the frontend should submit the form when the select changes and drop the "Update sort" button from src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:63-82, with a no-JavaScript fallback that keeps the button visible. If it is prototype incompleteness, the frontend is already right and this finding is struck.
finding.falsifiedBy: A Design release 1 dashboard capture in which changing the "Sort by" select re-orders the list without any further action by the user.
finding.verification: Ran the falsifier as far as it can be run from a static corpus and then went to the source, which settles it more cheaply. dr1-dashboard.html contains exactly one <form> — the results toolbar holding the sort select — and its only <button> elements are the service-navigation toggle and the two MoJ date pickers' own controls, so there is no submit anywhere near the select and the filter inputs are not even inside a form. Read app/views/dashboard.html:230-251 and src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:63-82. Listed app/assets/javascripts: 21 files, and the 5 that contain the string "sort" are all search widgets (country, commodity, airport, transit-country, address-book-lookup) sorting their own result arrays; none touches the dashboard. Opened evidence/prototype@491b3926/page/dr1-dashboard.png (select alone, no button) and evidence/frontend@76a864ba/page/fe-dashboard-populated.png ("Update sort" immediately right of the select). The disputed banding survives.
finding.correction: The banding and the settling question are right and are kept. One sentence in the difference slot was factually wrong and has been fixed: it said "the prototype's dashboard route does read a sort query parameter and apply it". It reads it and does not apply it. getDashboardViewModel builds its visible list by tab, filter and page slice only, and the entire file contains just two .sort( calls, one on address names and one on a label list, neither reachable from the dashboard. That makes the case for disputing stronger rather than weaker — Design release 1's select demonstrably re-orders nothing at all, so its missing button is no evidence either way about apply-on-change. The toolbar citation was also a few lines short — it started at the select's label rather than at the <form> that holds the count and the select — and now reads app/views/dashboard.html:231-251, which is the whole toolbar the sentence describes.

relatedTo.why: Same control; one is what the options say and the other is how the choice is applied.
